summary.one_line: A Mumbai-focused, family-controlled residential developer with a large legacy land bank and rising pre-sales. It is raising Rs.500 crore, all fresh issue and mostly to repay debt, but still carries heavy leverage, has had negative operating cash flow in each of the last three years, and has related-party transactions that its own auditors flagged as prejudicial. Worth tracking, not applying.
bull_points: Sales bookings (pre-sales) grew from Rs.15,276.41 million in FY24 to Rs.18,990.49 million in FY25 and Rs.23,535.05 million in FY26. Gross collections were Rs.18,546.13 million in FY26 (S1).

The land bank is large and mostly owned: 88.37 million sq ft of developable area, of which 56.41 million sq ft is upcoming projects (S1). About 94.56% of developable area is greenfield land (S9), including a 250-acre township at Dombivli and a 36-acre site at Kanjurmarg East (S9).
It ranked #1 in sales in Mumbai's eastern suburbs (7.88% share) and #1 in new launches in Kalyan-Dombivli (11.41% share) between January 2023 and March 2026, per the JLL industry report (S5, S7).
The issue is 100% fresh, with no offer for sale. Rs.325 crore of the Rs.500 crore is earmarked for debt repayment at the parent and its subsidiaries (S1, S4).
Profitability improved: EBITDA margin rose from 8.37% in FY24 to 19.44% in FY26, and PAT went from Rs.937.00 million to Rs.1,857.63 million (S1).
bear_points: Operating cash flow was negative in all three years: Rs.(5,494.82) million in FY24, Rs.(1,981.36) million in FY25 and Rs.(1,807.13) million in FY26, against cumulative restated PAT of about Rs.3,351 million (S1).

Total borrowings rose from Rs.17,836.50 million to Rs.29,091.28 million over FY24-FY26, and net debt/equity was 3.29x at FY26. The Rs.3,250 million debt repayment covers only about 11% of borrowings (S1).
Statutory auditors identified related-party transactions by the company and by Runwal Residency as prejudicial to the interest of the entity concerned (S1, S24).
Contingent liabilities are Rs.7,980.08 crore (S9, S10). Outstanding claims against the company alone total Rs.13,663.13 million, and subsidiaries face 85 tax and 61 real-estate matters (S1).
About 66.65% of projects are in Mumbai, and 7,072 units (7.55 million sq ft) are unsold across completed and ongoing projects (S1).
watch_points: Whether operating cash flow turns positive after listing. This is the single test of whether the pre-sales growth converts to cash (S1).
Disclosure and clean-up of the related-party dealings the auditors flagged (S1).
Progress on the 59.43 acres reported to be under investigation over government land classification (S10).
Brand overlap and absence of a non-compete with the separately run Runwal Realty / Runwal Developers, which has its own Rs.2,000 crore IPO filing (S17, S18, S21).
Day-1 subscription data was not yet available at the time of writing. Treat any later figures, and the unofficial GMP (Rs.17-37 range, S12), as sentiment only.

reasoning: The money mostly shrinks debt rather than building a moat. Rs.325 crore of the Rs.500 crore fresh issue repays borrowings, against Rs.2,909 crore of total debt (S1, S4). Pro-forma net debt/equity would still be well above 1.5x on our rough calculation from the FY26 figures, so the company stays a leveraged developer after the IPO.

The growth story has not yet become cash. Pre-sales grew about 54% over FY24-FY26, but operating cash flow was negative every year: a cumulative outflow of about Rs.9,283 million, while restated PAT totalled about Rs.3,351 million (S1). Until collections run ahead of land and construction spend, reported profit overstates what equity holders can actually get.

Governance is the deciding negative. The company's own statutory auditors flagged related-party transactions at the parent and at Runwal Residency as prejudicial to the entity (S1). The promoter group will still own about 84.6% after the issue (S4), and related entities in the same business have no non-compete (S21). Minority shareholders would have limited protection.

The land bank is a real asset, but it is not a durable moat. Leadership in the eastern suburbs and Kalyan-Dombivli (S7) rests on legacy land. Runwal is #3 in Mumbai with only about a 2.3-2.5% share (S7). It competes with much larger listed players and with a family-linked developer that uses the same surname brand (S8, S17).

The litigation and contingent-liability load is heavy for the company's size. Contingent liabilities are Rs.7,980 crore (S9), claims against the company total Rs.13,663 million (S1), and the land-title investigation covers 59.43 acres (S10). Any of these could change the economics of individual projects.

Tracking is better than applying now. A year or two of listed quarterly disclosure would show whether operating cash flow turns positive and whether related-party dealings are cleaned up. If both happen, the land bank and pre-sales momentum could justify a fresh look.

subsections.title: What Runwal Enterprises does and how it earns revenue

blocks.text: Runwal Enterprises is a real estate developer. It builds residential projects in the affordable, mid-income and luxury segments, plus commercial spaces, retail malls and educational buildings. It reports a single operating segment, real estate development, and substantially all revenue comes from India (S1). The company was incorporated in February 2016 (S7), originally as Propel Developers Private Limited (S9). It was later renamed Runwal Apartments Private Limited and then Runwal Enterprises (S1). It is the Subodh Runwal half of the Runwal group, which Subhash Runwal founded in 1978 and which split into two independent businesses in 2016 (S15).

The economics are those of a for-sale developer. Units are sold off-plan during construction, which generates 'sales value' (bookings) and collections. Revenue is recognised only once the occupancy certificate is received and possession is handed over (S10). That is why reported revenue swings sharply from year to year: Rs.24,088.65 million in FY24, Rs.10,077.66 million in FY25 and Rs.17,989.49 million in FY26 (S1). Revenue tracks completions (deliveries of 2.23, 1.33 and 1.17 million sq ft), not current selling activity (S1). Bookings are the better guide to the underlying business.

blocks.caption: Operating KPIs, FY24-FY26 (Source: RHP via abridged prospectus, S1)

blocks.text: Bookings grew about 54% over two years, but the gains came from both volume (area sold +28% in FY26) and price (average realisation +25% from FY24 to FY25, then slightly lower in FY26) (S1). Collections were lower in FY26 than in FY24 even though bookings were far higher (S1). That gap matters for the cash-flow discussion in the financials section.

subsections.title: Portfolio, scale and where it operates

blocks.text: At March 31, 2026 the company had 19 completed, 28 ongoing and 33 upcoming projects, with an aggregate developable area of 88.37 million sq ft (S1). Of that area, completed projects account for 12.09 million sq ft (13.68%), ongoing projects 19.88 million sq ft (22.49%) and upcoming projects 56.41 million sq ft (63.83%) (S1). Residential makes up 74.58 million sq ft and non-residential 13.80 million sq ft (S1). Residential projects account for 84.39% of developable area and 93.93% of total sales (S1).

Geography is almost entirely Mumbai. All completed, ongoing and upcoming projects are in Mumbai, except two upcoming projects near Alibaug (S1). Brokers summarising the RHP describe the footprint as Mumbai's eastern, central, western and peripheral suburbs (S5). Flagship developments include Runwal Gardens and Runwal My City in Dombivli, a township of about 250 acres, and Runwal Bliss and Runwal Avenue at Kanjurmarg East, on about 36 acres (S9). Other named brands include Runwal Greens, 7 Mahalaxmi and a Girgaum project (S5).

blocks.caption: Developable area by project stage, March 31, 2026 (S1)

blocks.text: Two-thirds of the portfolio has not been launched yet. That is visibility of future supply, but it also means most of the value depends on approvals, launches and construction that have not happened. The company had 1,181 permanent employees (S8).

Customers are individual home buyers plus, for the non-residential portfolio, commercial office users, retail tenants and schools (S1). The company says it has no material customer concentration, and no single customer was a significant share of revenue in FY24-FY26 (S1). That is normal for a housing developer and removes one risk category.

There are no manufacturing facilities. Operating locations are the project sites and the Sion head office (S1). Construction is carried out with in-house functional teams and tie-ups with external design and architecture firms (S1). The abridged prospectus does not name specific contractors or material suppliers, and we could not open the full RHP chapter on suppliers, so supplier concentration cannot be assessed here.

items: Land model: mostly owned greenfield land (94.56% of developable area per S9). The stated strategy adds asset-light growth through redevelopment, joint ventures and joint development agreements (S1).
Revenue model: off-plan sales with stage-linked collections. Revenue is recognised on completion and handover (S10).
Funding model: construction and land are funded with a mix of customer advances and debt. Net debt was Rs.27,781.10 million at FY26 (S1).
Pricing: brokers cite a claimed premium to micro-market averages of about 3% in Kanjurmarg, 2% in Mulund and 13% in Dombivli (S10).

blocks.text: According to the JLL report commissioned for the offer, residential sales in India's top seven markets hit a record 321,518 units in calendar 2024, with 313,051 units launched (S1). In calendar 2025, launches reached 96% of the 2024 level and sales reached 89% of it (S1). In other words, 2025 sales declined about 11% from the peak even though JLL describes the phase as 'accelerated growth'. Over CY2023 to March 2026, the top seven markets averaged about 299,800 unit sales and about 307,200 unit launches a year (S1).

Mumbai is the largest market. It accounted for about 24% of top-seven sales and launches from January 2023 to March 2026 and about 23% of sales value (S1). Average capital values in Mumbai were Rs.15,145 per sq ft of saleable area in March 2026, the highest of the seven markets (S1). Runwal's own average realisation of Rs.11,366 per sq ft in FY26 is below that city average (S1). This fits its skew toward the eastern suburbs and the Kalyan-Dombivli periphery rather than the island city.

The cycle is mature. Volumes are at or just past record highs, and 2025 sales were below 2024 (S1). A developer that still has negative operating cash flow at this point in the cycle has less room to absorb a downturn.

blocks.caption: Market-share claims, January 2023 to March 2026 (JLL, as cited by S7 and S9)

blocks.text: Listed competitors used in the RHP's peer set include Macrotech (Lodha), Prestige Estates, Oberoi Realty and Godrej Properties (S8), plus Sunteck Realty (S9). All of them are far bigger by revenue. For example, Lodha reported Rs.166,762 million and Godrej Rs.51,314 million against Runwal's Rs.17,989 million (S8). An unusually direct competitor is Runwal Developers (brand: Runwal Realty), run by the promoter's brother Sandeep Runwal since the 2016 split (S15, S16). It also develops in Mumbai under the Runwal name and has filed its own Rs.2,000 crore IPO draft with SEBI (S17, S18).

The market-share metrics shifted between the draft and the final offer document. The March 2025 DRHP reportedly claimed 2nd place in launches (5.69%) and sales (5.25%) since January 2019 (S13). The RHP instead claims 3rd place with about 2.3-2.5% for January 2023 to March 2026 (S7). The two figures use different periods and possibly different geographic bases. The later figures are the more conservative, and they are the ones this report relies on.

There is no real technical or regulatory moat. Residential development in Mumbai is fragmented, and a 2.3-2.5% city share (S7) is not market power. The only durable advantage is the land bank. Large contiguous greenfield parcels bought long ago, such as the roughly 250-acre Dombivli township and the roughly 36-acre Kanjurmarg site (S9), would be expensive or impossible to assemble today in a city with Rs.15,145 per sq ft average capital values (S1). This is a real asset advantage. It explains the leading share in the eastern suburbs and Kalyan-Dombivli (S7), but it is finite and gets used up as projects are sold.

The brand claim is weaker than it looks. The Runwal name is shared with an independently controlled family developer (S15). Anything that damages the 'Runwal' brand at either company can hurt the other, and a snippet of the DRHP indicates that group entities in similar lines of business are not bound by non-compete agreements (S21). The prospectus's other claimed strengths are standard for the sector: 'well-established brand', 'premium pricing' and 'township core competency' (S1).
Verdict on moat: a valuable legacy land bank, but no structural barrier. Returns will depend on execution and on the Mumbai cycle.

blocks.caption: Restated consolidated financials, Rs. million (S1)
rows: Adjusted EBITDA margin (adds back finance cost in cost of sales)

blocks.text: The revenue line is lumpy because it follows handovers, not sales. FY24 revenue was more than twice FY26 revenue on a lower gross margin (S1). Profit improved over the period. FY26 PAT of Rs.1,857.63 million was about three times FY25 and about twice FY24 (S1). Gross margin also moved from about 20% to 33-36%, which suggests a mix shift toward higher-margin projects being completed (S1). The gap between reported EBITDA margin (19.44%) and adjusted EBITDA margin (32.92%) in FY26 shows how much interest is capitalised into inventory and then released through cost of sales (S1). Interest is a large real cost that the headline EBITDA partly hides.

The restated perimeter appears to have changed since the draft. Groww's summary of the March 2025 DRHP put FY24 revenue at Rs.662.19 crore (S13), while the RHP restated FY24 at Rs.2,408.87 crore (S1). We could not open either full document to reconcile the two. The likely explanation is that group entities were brought into the consolidation (or were consolidated differently). The RHP figures are used throughout, but the history is less comparable than it looks.

subsections.title: Balance sheet, leverage and cash flow

blocks.caption: Balance sheet and cash flow, Rs. million (S1)

blocks.text: The key red flag is the cash/profit mismatch. Over FY24-FY26 the company reported about Rs.3,351 million of PAT but consumed about Rs.9,283 million in operations (our sums from S1). The gap was filled by borrowing: financing inflows totalled about Rs.11,576 million over three years, and gross debt rose by Rs.11,255 million (S1). For a developer this usually means money is being tied up in land, approvals and work-in-progress faster than customers are paying. In FY26 collections of Rs.18,546 million trailed bookings of Rs.23,535 million (S1). Negative operating cash flow is not unusual for a fast-growing developer, but three straight years of it at this scale means the business has not yet shown it can fund itself.

Net worth rose Rs.3,123 million in FY26 against PAT of Rs.1,858 million (S1). That points to fresh equity during the year. The RHP records share transactions in the preceding year (S1), and HDFC Capital Affordable Real Estate Fund-3 is the only material non-promoter holder at 4.83% (S1). This helped bring net debt/equity down from 4.64x to 3.29x, but the absolute debt kept rising (S1). Brokers also report contingent liabilities of Rs.7,980.08 crore at March 2026, mostly guarantees and disputed tax claims (S9, S10). That is very large relative to net worth of Rs.768 crore.

Three years of negative operating cash flow, rising gross debt, net debt/equity of 3.3x and contingent liabilities about ten times net worth (S1, S9) make this a stretched balance sheet. The IPO proceeds help, but they do not fix it.

subsections.title: Does the trend support the growth story?

blocks.text: Partly. The trends that support the story are real. Bookings compounded about 24% a year from FY24 to FY26, units sold rose from 1,688 to 2,182, launches recovered to 2.06 million sq ft in FY26, and margins widened (S1). The trends that undercut it are equally real. Deliveries fell three years in a row, from 2.23 to 1.17 million sq ft. Revenue in FY26 was still below FY24. Unsold inventory stands at 7,072 units, or 7.55 million sq ft (S1). And the business has not generated operating cash in any of the three years (S1).

items: Falling deliveries against rising bookings point to a construction backlog. Future revenue should rise if execution holds, but execution risk is also rising (S1).
Average realisation fell slightly in FY26 (Rs.11,366 vs Rs.11,754 per sq ft) even as volumes rose (S1). This may reflect product mix, but it is not evidence of pricing power.
Eleven subsidiaries had negative net worth in at least one of FY24-FY26, and more reported losses (S1). The consolidated profit sits alongside weak pockets inside the group.

blocks.text: The growth story is supported on bookings and margins, but not on cash. A retail investor should treat the FY26 profit jump as a result of project completions, not proof of a cash-generative franchise.

sections.title: Issue details and objects of the issue

blocks.caption: Key issue terms (S1, S4, S5)
rows: 100% fresh issue; no offer for sale (S14, S22)
Up to Rs.5,000 million (Rs.499.83 crore; about 1.64 crore shares)
Rs.290-305 per share (face value Rs.2); see note below
Anchor Sep 24, 2026; open Sep 25; close Sep 29, 2026
QIB up to 50%, NII at least 15%, retail at least 35%
ICICI Securities, Jefferies India / MUFG Intime India

blocks.text: The task brief gave the price band as Rs.290-302. Every source we could open (the company's press release, broker pages and news) states Rs.290-305 (S4, S5, S6). This report uses Rs.290-305 as the sourced figure. Readers should check the final band on the exchange bid form.

The offer has been cut back and restructured since the draft. The March 2025 DRHP proposed a Rs.1,000 crore fresh issue, with at least 75% reserved for QIBs and at most 10% for retail (S13, S20). That allocation implies filing under Regulation 6(2), the route for companies that do not meet the track-record tests. The RHP halves the size to Rs.500 crore and files under Regulation 6(1), with 35% for retail (S1, S6). Nothing in the documents we saw explains why the size was halved.

blocks.caption: Use of net proceeds (S1; balance per S10)
rows: Investment in wholly owned material subsidiaries Runwal Residency Pvt Ltd and Evie Real Estate Pvt Ltd to repay/prepay their borrowings
Funding acquisitions of future real estate projects + general corporate purposes
Balance (up to about 1,750, less issue expenses)
capped at 35% combined; each capped at 25%

blocks.text: About 65% of the gross proceeds (Rs.3,250 million) goes to debt repayment, a third of it at the parent and two-thirds at two subsidiaries (S1). The March 2025 draft had proposed Rs.200 crore of parent debt repayment and Rs.450 crore for subsidiaries, including Susneh Infrapark (per search-result summaries of DRHP coverage, S13, S20; draft filed with SEBI, S3). The RHP drops Susneh from the list of beneficiaries and halves both amounts (S1). Evie Real Estate, one of the two subsidiaries receiving money, has no credit rating for its borrowings and made a loss in FY25 (S1).

The remaining roughly Rs.1,750 million is effectively a blank cheque. It is for 'acquisitions of future real estate projects' that are not identified, plus general corporate purposes. Together they are capped at 35% of the gross issue, and each individually at 25% (S1). Investors are therefore funding land purchases they cannot evaluate.
Scale check: Rs.3,250 million of debt repayment is about 11% of FY26 borrowings of Rs.29,091 million (S1). The issue lowers interest costs at the margin but leaves the balance sheet heavily geared.

subsections.title: Fresh issue vs OFS: what it means for investors

blocks.text: Because there is no offer for sale, every rupee raised goes to the company, net of issue expenses (S1, S4). The promoter is not selling. Subodh Runwal holds 80.89% directly and the promoter group another 14.27% (S1). The promoter acquired no shares in the last three years and his weighted-average cost of acquisition is shown as nil (S1). This is better alignment than an OFS-heavy deal, where existing holders cash out.

The flip side is that the promoter group will still control about 84.6% after listing (S4). Free float will be small, around 15%, which limits both liquidity and the power of minority shareholders in any vote on related-party matters.

items: Positive: no OFS, and all proceeds go toward the balance sheet (S1).
Neutral: debt repayment improves ratios but creates no new earning assets (S1).
Negative: about a third of the issue funds unspecified acquisitions and general purposes (S1).

blocks.text: The sole promoter is Subodh Subhash Runwal, 51, Chairman and Managing Director. He has a commerce degree from R.A. Podar College (University of Mumbai) and an MBA from Northeastern University, Boston. He has 31 years of real-estate experience and was previously associated with Wheelabrator Alloy Castings, Runwal Residency and Runwal Apartments (S1). He is the son of group founder Subhash Runwal, who began developing in Mumbai in 1978. Since the 2016 split, Subodh has run Runwal Enterprises and his brother Sandeep has run Runwal Realty (S15, S16).

The shareholding is highly concentrated. The promoter holds 80.89%. Father Subhash (7.61%) and mother Chanda Runwal (6.66%) hold most of the rest of the promoter group's 14.27%. HDFC Capital Affordable Real Estate Fund-3, at 4.83%, is the only material outside holder (S1). HDFC Capital's presence as a pre-IPO investor is some institutional validation, but it is a real-estate credit/equity fund with its own exit horizon.

This is not a routine RPT profile. Among its top ten risk factors, the RHP discloses that the company and its subsidiary Runwal Residency previously entered into related-party transactions which the statutory auditors identified as prejudicial to the interest of the entity concerned. The company also says it may continue to enter into related-party transactions involving conflicts of interest (S1). Broker reviews repeat the same auditor flag (S24). An auditor explicitly calling transactions 'prejudicial' is a serious finding. The abridged prospectus does not identify the counterparties or amounts, and we could not open the full RHP RPT schedule, so we cannot quantify it.

items: Statutory auditors and subsidiary/JV auditors included remarks in their audit and examination reports (S1). The RHP says there are no unadjusted qualifications in the restated financials (S1).
A DRHP snippet indicates that promoter-group and group companies operate in similar lines of business without non-compete agreements, creating potential conflicts of interest (S21).

The group company Runwal Developers Limited is involved in litigation that the RHP singles out as potentially material to the company (S1). It is the separately controlled Runwal Realty business, which has its own IPO filing (S17).
Contingent liabilities of Rs.7,980.08 crore include personal/corporate guarantees, some of which may relate to group entities (S9, S10). Counterparty detail was not available to us.

blocks.text: Auditor-flagged prejudicial RPTs, a shared family brand with no non-compete, and about 84.6% post-issue promoter control (S1, S4, S21) together form the main governance concern. It is serious enough to weigh against applying.

The litigation load is heavy for a company with net worth of Rs.7,682 million (S1). Claims against the company alone are about 1.8 times net worth (our calculation), although quantified claims rarely resolve at face value. The six criminal matters against the promoter and the 61 RERA/REAT matters against subsidiaries are particularly relevant. The RERA matters are typically buyer complaints over delays or deliverables. The promoter is not subject to any SEBI or stock-exchange disciplinary action (S1). Separately, brokers report that about 59.43 acres are under investigation over government land classification (S10).

items: Persistent negative operating cash flow: Rs.(5,494.82) million, Rs.(1,981.36) million and Rs.(1,807.13) million in FY24-FY26, funded by debt (S1). If sales slow, the funding gap widens quickly.
Leverage: borrowings of Rs.29,091.28 million and net debt/equity of 3.29x at FY26 (S1). The IPO retires about 11%.
Related-party transactions flagged by auditors as prejudicial at the company and at Runwal Residency (S1).
Contingent liabilities of Rs.7,980.08 crore (S9), roughly ten times FY26 net worth (S1).
Weak subsidiaries: several reported losses or negative net worth in FY24-FY26. Evie Real Estate, a recipient of IPO money, is unrated and loss-making in FY25 (S1).

blocks.text: Any of these would individually warrant caution. Together they define the investment case.

items: Execution: 28 ongoing and 33 upcoming projects make up 86.33% of developable area (S1). Deliveries fell from 2.23 to 1.17 million sq ft over FY24-FY26 (S1).
Unsold inventory: 7,072 units, or 7.55 million sq ft, across completed and ongoing projects (S1). Holding costs rise with time.
Single-city concentration: 66.65% of projects are in Mumbai, and all but two are in or around the city (S1). A Mumbai-specific slowdown or policy change would hit directly.
Land title and acquisition: the RHP flags title and land-acquisition risk (S1), and about 59.43 acres are reported to be under a government land-classification investigation (S10).
Cycle risk: top-seven residential sales in CY2025 were 89% of the CY2024 peak (S1).

blocks.text: Customer or supplier concentration is not a meaningful risk here, because there is no material customer concentration (S1). The risks that matter are the cash, leverage and governance ones above, plus execution on a pipeline that is mostly still unbuilt.

The concrete forward statements we could find are the stated strategies in the offer document. They are to stay focused on Mumbai; to pursue asset-light growth through redevelopment, joint ventures and joint development; to keep serving all residential segments while selectively adding retail, commercial and mixed-use; and to expand IT-driven processes (S1). Coverage around the launch framed the IPO as a move to strengthen the balance sheet (S19).

We found no specific guidance on pre-sales, launches, deliveries, debt targets or margins in an interview, investor call or press statement. We did not have access to the full MD&A chapter of the RHP. The press release restates historical figures and market-share rankings rather than giving targets (S5). With no management targets available, the outlook below is our reading of the disclosed pipeline, not company guidance.
No concrete forward guidance from management was found. Treat broker 'subscribe' notes (e.g. S7) as sell-side opinion, not company outlook.

The pipeline is large. Upcoming projects total 56.41 million sq ft (S1), against FY26 sales of 2.07 million sq ft and launches of 2.06 million sq ft (S1). At the current pace that is decades of supply, so the constraint is execution and capital, not land. Falling deliveries alongside rising bookings suggest completions, and therefore reported revenue, should pick up if construction keeps pace (S1). That would ease the cash drag.

items: Upside: lower interest after the IPO debt repayment, more launches from the owned land bank, and completion-led revenue recognition (S1).
Downside: a softer Mumbai market (CY2025 sales below CY2024, S1), capital intensity of new launches, and land-acquisition spending from the unallocated issue proceeds (S1).
Key metric to watch: operating cash flow and collections versus bookings in the first reported half-years after listing (S1).

subsections.title: Subscription, anchors and grey market (as of opening day)

blocks.text: This report was written on September 25, 2026, the day the issue opened. The subscription trackers we checked had not yet posted meaningful day-1 figures and showed 0.00x for QIB, NII and retail at their last update (S11). We therefore report no subscription multiple. Figures published later on day 1 will be partial, and they are not a signal of business quality.

Anchor bidding was scheduled for September 24, 2026 (S1). When we checked, the trackers said anchor allocations had not yet been announced (S11), and we found no published list of anchor investors, amounts or lock-in terms. Under standard SEBI rules, anchors are locked in for 30 days on half of their allocation and 90 days on the rest, but we could not confirm the specific allotment.

blocks.caption: Unofficial grey market premium reports (not an investment signal)
rows: Rs.37 (range Rs.17-37 over the prior sessions)

blocks.text: GMP is unofficial, unregulated and inconsistent across sources (Rs.17-37). It says nothing about the cash-flow, leverage or governance issues above and has no bearing on the verdict.

method: Primary source: the 10-page abridged prospectus (a summary of the RHP dated September 21, 2026), downloaded from SEBI's public-issues RHP filing page (S1, S2) and read page by page.
